headline: The AI selloff became a market selloff: on Thursday the Nasdaq 100 fell into a correction in one day and chips had their worst day since March 2020, and this morning October jobs came in strong at 165,000 against 59,000 expected.
summary: The dashboard is still behind: prices_as_of is 2026-11-04, so every Nov 5 level here comes from Massive. On Thursday SPY fell 4.41% to 733.00 and QQQ 6.49% to 647.05, which is 14.8% under its Oct 6 record and well through the 10% correction line near 683.69; the chip ETF SMH fell 11.21%. This time the AI buyers fell too (Microsoft 3.58%, Amazon 2.19%), so Wednesday's split between AI buyers and AI suppliers did not hold. The jobs report came out at 8:30am ET: 165,000 jobs, unemployment 4.1% and wages up 3.1% from a year ago, all stronger than expected (BLS). Before the open Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 1.4% and Dow futures down about 0.9%, with the 10 year near 4.88% (Yahoo). The put screen passes nothing: ADI and SNAP fell out of their zones, AFRM fell after its report, and the GD, LDOS, AEP and COF puts barely trade.

regime.why: A 6.49% one day drop in QQQ on heavy volume is distribution, not a dip, and the selling spread from AI power to chips to the big buyers. A strong jobs report and wages above forecast keep a December Fed hike on the table, so there is no rate cut cushion. Oil is back near $97 on new tanker attacks.

signals.title: Nasdaq 100 drops through its 10% correction line in one day
signals.since_yesterday: QQQ fell 6.49% on Nov 5 to 647.05, 14.8% under its record; on Nov 4 it was back above the 10% line.
signals.what_happened: Nov 5 closes (Massive): SPY 733.00 (-4.41%), QQQ 647.05 (-6.49%, on 130.7 million shares), DIA 514.27 (-3.53%), IWM 270.98 (-4.59%), SMH 447.73 (-11.21%), SOXX 131.90 (-12.15%). The S&P 500 index closed at 7,353.73, down 4.36%, its worst day since April 2025, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% and closed in a correction (CNBC). The VIX touched 28.09, its highest since March 31 (CNBC). CNBC tied the drop to fears that a Democratic Congress and new governors will slow data center building and add AI rules; Caterpillar fell 6% and JPMorgan 4%. QQQ's 10% line is about 683.69 and its 20% line about 607.73 (my math from the 759.66 record).
signals.so_what: Wednesday looked like a rotation: money left the AI suppliers and went into the AI buyers. Thursday broke that story, because Microsoft, Amazon, Apple and Alphabet fell too. When everything falls on heavy volume, funds are cutting risk, not picking winners. Who pays: anyone who bought the AI build with borrowed money or options. What becomes scarce: buyers willing to step in before the facts change. What would make this wrong: a quick policy signal that a national data center pause will not pass (the Sanders bill has been seen as a near impossible sell since March) and a strong rebound day on heavier volume than Thursday.
signals.for_you: Swing: no new longs while the index sits under its correction line; a one day bounce in futures is not a turn. Puts: premiums are rich because risk is real; the screen below passes nothing. Long term: wait for the dashboard's refresh; names that fell under their zones (ADI, NVDA, AMD) need the chart to stop falling first.

signals.title: Chips have their worst day since March 2020; the selling reaches memory, Korea and the deal names
signals.since_yesterday: The data center limits selloff moved from power and neoclouds to the chip makers and to Asia: AMD and Micron fell more than 17% and the KOSPI tripped a circuit breaker this morning.
signals.what_happened: Nov 5 closes (Massive): Nvidia 181.60 (-9.26%, 306 million shares), AMD 404.40 (-17.26%), Micron 656.39 (-17.46%), SanDisk 806.43 (-22.26%), Broadcom 291.53 (-10.43%), Arm 166.72 (-13.08%), TSMC ADR 353.10 (-10.78%), Astera Labs 179.47 (-19.62%), Marvell 133.55 (-16.43%), Lumentum 509.70 (-18.68%), Qualcomm 156.75 (-9.49%, 40.2 million shares). The AI power names fell again: Vertiv 176.73 (-14.02%), Quanta 509.06 (-12.30%), Bloom 167.52 (-16.41%), GE Vernova 770.51 (-7.48%), CoreWeave 43.66 (-9.83%). Astera had just reported Q3 revenue of $584.9 million, up 154%, and EPS of $1.05, both above estimates (company figures via Simply Wall St). At 4.5 Marvell shares per Lumentum share the deal is worth 600.98, so LITE trades 15.2% below it (my math). In Seoul the KOSPI fell 6.02% to 5,059.69 on Nov 6 after a circuit breaker three minutes into trading; Samsung fell 6.35% and SK hynix 10.44% (Korea Herald, IBTimes). Before the open Nvidia traded near 189.68, up about 4.45% (Yahoo snapshot).
signals.so_what: Astera beat by a wide margin and still fell almost 20%. That says the selling is about who owns these stocks and how much risk they carry, not about this quarter's business. Second order: if funds keep cutting chips, the Korean and Taiwan markets, which are mostly memory and foundry, keep taking the worst of it, and the Marvell and Lumentum deal gap widens because Marvell's own price sets the deal's value. Third order: lower chip prices make new stock deals and debt for AI builders harder, which can slow orders a year from now even if demand holds. What would make this wrong: the next big chip reports showing orders still rising and the stocks closing up on them.
signals.for_you: Swing: no chip setups, and no buying the bounce until a base forms on lower volume. Puts: none in chips; a 17% day can repeat. Long term: NVDA (181.60) is now under its 198.26 zone bottom and AMD (404.40) under its 476.31 zone bottom, and both fail the 'not sliding' check, so neither is a buy now name. MRVL, LITE and QCOM have no buy verdict.

signals.title: October jobs: 165,000, nearly three times the forecast
signals.since_yesterday: The report is out: 165,000 jobs against a 59,000 Dow Jones forecast, unemployment 4.1%.
signals.what_happened: At 8:30am ET the Labor Department reported 165,000 jobs in October; the Dow Jones forecast was 59,000 and FactSet's 65,000. Unemployment fell to 4.1% from a 4.2% forecast. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% in the month to $38.00 and 3.1% from a year ago, above the 0.3% and 2.9% forecasts. August was revised up to 186,000 and September to 60,000. Professional and business services added 70,000, health care 42,000, transport 25,000 and manufacturing 19,000 (BLS, CNBC). After the report the 10 year traded near 4.876%, up about 0.04 point (Yahoo snapshot). On Nov 5, before the report, odds of a December Fed hike had fallen to 70.1% from 82.7% (CNBC).
signals.so_what: Good news for the economy is mixed news for stocks right now. Strong hiring and wages above forecast make it harder for the Fed to skip a December hike, and higher yields hurt the long duration tech stocks that just fell the most. It also says the selloff is not a recession call: the job market is not breaking. Health care hiring (42,000) keeps supporting hospital and clinic demand. What would make this wrong: the household survey or later revisions turning weak.
signals.for_you: Swing: the report removes one event; it does not fix the chart. Puts: the bar for any put is now about 4.88%. Long term: a strong economy supports the defensive buy zone names (GD, LDOS, AEP, COF) more than the chip names.

signals.title: Vistra beats and raises, the first test of the data center fear
signals.what_happened: Vistra reported this morning (Nov 6): adjusted EBITDA $2.378 billion, up more than 50%; GAAP net income $1.14 billion, including a $559 million unrealized hedge gain; 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance narrowed to $7.1 to $7.5 billion with a higher midpoint; first 2027 guidance of $7.7 to $8.5 billion; a new $1.5 billion buyback; and a 20 year, 207 MW power deal with New Era Energy and Digital at its Odessa, Texas gas plant (SEC 8-K). Revenue of $6.35 billion missed the $6.79 billion estimate. Shares rose about 5% premarket (Investing.com). VST closed 112.89 on Nov 5, down 6.15%, after a 13.83% drop on Nov 4 (Massive).
signals.so_what: The market sold Vistra on the fear that Texas will slow data centers. The company answered with a higher 2027 outlook and a new Texas data center contract signed anyway. That is the key question for the whole AI power group: does the permit fear show up in signed contracts? For now, no. Second order: if power producers keep signing, the buyers of power (data center owners) keep paying higher prices, which is the political fight in the first place. What would make this wrong: a state level pause that blocks new interconnections in Texas.
signals.for_you: Swing: no VST setup; one good report does not end a 20% two day drop. Wait for a base. Puts: none in the AI power group yet. Long term: VST has no buy verdict.

signals.title: Earnings: Affirm and MP beat; Affirm falls, AppLovin and Airbnb jump, Expedia and Remitly drop
signals.since_yesterday: Affirm and MP Materials reported after Thursday's close.
signals.what_happened: Affirm (fiscal Q1): GMV $14.4 billion, up 34%; revenue about $1.26 billion, up about 35%; full year GMV outlook raised to more than $65.25 billion from more than $64 billion; Q2 revenue guide $1.435 to $1.465 billion. Management called 30% GMV growth a floor for the year. The stock fell about 9% after hours to about 63.43 (Benzinga) after closing at 69.66, down 7.84% (Massive). MP Materials: revenue $147.7 million, up 176%; NdPr output 1,018 tonnes, up 41%; GM magnet qualification done, with paid deliveries starting in Q4 (SEC 8-K). MP closed 33.74 (-6.04%) and rose about 2.6% after hours (Benzinga). Other Nov 5 closes (Massive): AppLovin 356.10 (+31.04%) after its report; Expedia 272.48 (-13.74%) after weak guidance (CNBC); Remitly 21.545 (-20.44%, 11.5 million shares), a day after it beat and raised; the reason was not found. Airbnb reported Q3 revenue of $4.9 billion, up 19% (SEC 8-K), and traded near 193.40 premarket, up 13.68% (Yahoo).
signals.so_what: Good results are not enough in a falling market unless growth speeds up. Affirm grew 34% and raised its outlook, but 'at least 30%' for the year means slower growth ahead, and fintech was already falling (Robinhood -10.32%, Coinbase -9.69% on Nov 5). MP is the opposite case: a small company crossing into real magnet sales four days before China's export pause ends on Nov 10. Remitly's 20% drop after a beat and a bigger buyback is a warning sign we cannot yet explain.
signals.for_you: Puts: AFRM's report is out, so it was screened, but the after hours price is under its 64.54 zone bottom and the group is falling; no AFRM put. Long term: AFRM was 'Buy zone now' on Nov 4 closes; treat it as a watch name until the dashboard rechecks the chart. MP: no setup or verdict; watch Nov 10.

signals.title: Oil bounces back near $98 on new tanker attacks; energy stocks keep falling
signals.since_yesterday: Brent rose 3.88% on Nov 5 after Iran said two tankers and a tug caught fire in Hormuz, but XLE fell 2.98%.
signals.what_happened: Brent's January contract settled at $98.29, up $3.67 (3.88%), and WTI at $90.52, up $2.40 (Reuters). Iran's Revolutionary Guard said two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire after trying unauthorized routes through the strait. Reuters also reported that Iran sent a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar. Early Friday Brent was $96.93 at 4:38am ET after nearly reaching $100; Rapidan's Bob McNally puts the chance of renewed fighting at 80% (CNBC). Reuters' $3.67 gain implies a Nov 4 settle of $94.62, not the $93.52 we used yesterday; Reuters is the stronger source, so treat Wednesday's figure as about $94.6. Energy stocks did not follow oil up: XOM 165.30 (-2.35%), CVX 212.93 (-1.86%), COP 135.46 (-1.08%), EOG 144.89 (-1.48%) (Massive).
signals.so_what: Oil now swings $4 to $10 a day on each headline, and energy stocks are trading with the broad market, not with crude. That combination is the worst one for a swing trader: the stock can fall on a day oil rises. Who gets paid: tanker owners and insurers on each attack. What would make the war premium vanish: a signed deal through Qatar; what would spike it: renewed strikes.
signals.for_you: Swing: the four oil plans closed by the stop rule on Nov 4 (treat them as closed). On Nov 5 all four closed below their old stops (XOM 169.99, CVX 218.23, COP 135.75, EOG 147.98), so the rule kept losses smaller. No re-entry until oil bases and a fresh dashboard setup appears. Puts: none on energy.

cycle.quadrant_why: October added 165,000 jobs with unemployment at 4.1% and wages up 3.1% from a year ago, above forecast (BLS, Nov 6). Q3 GDP grew at a 3.4% pace and core PCE was 3.1% (Oct 29 data). Brent is back near $97 to $98 after Wednesday's drop, so the oil relief to inflation lasted one day.
cycle.short_term_debt_cycle: Tightening, late. The Fed's range is 3.75% to 4.00% since Oct 28, and before the jobs report markets put about 70% odds on a December hike (CNBC, Nov 5). Today's strong report makes a skip harder. The 10 year is near 4.88%.
cycle.long_term_debt_cycle: Late. US debt is above $40 trillion, and the AI build now leans on stock and debt markets that just fell hard. Falling chip prices raise the cost of that funding.
cycle.big_cycle: Internal order: the split government now reaches the market through state and federal data center politics. External order: Iran is attacking tankers while talking through Qatar. Technology: AI results are still strong (Astera, Vistra), but prices are being set by fear of rules, not by results.
tailwinds: The job market is strong; this is not a recession selloff.
AI suppliers still report rising orders (Vistra's 2027 outlook, Astera's 154% growth).
Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 1.4% before the open.
headwinds: A strong jobs report keeps a December hike on the table.
Chips and Asian chip markets are falling on heavy volume.
Oil swings $4 to $10 a day on Iran headlines.

history.what: The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.97% on April 3 and 5.82% on April 4 after broad tariffs were announced, then rose 12.16% on April 9 when most were paused.
history.lesson: A policy driven crash can reverse fast when the policy changes, and the people who sold at the low missed the rebound. But no one knew the pause date in advance.

history.when: March 2000 to October 2002: the telecom build bust
history.what: The Nasdaq Composite peaked at 5,048.62 on March 10, 2000 and fell about 78% by October 2002, as the build out of fiber and networks ran ahead of profits and the suppliers fell hardest.
history.lesson: When investors doubt the buyers will keep spending, the suppliers to the build fall first and furthest, even while they still report growth.

cycle.differences: Unlike 2000, today's big AI buyers (Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet) are profitable and pay for most of the build from cash flow, and the threat is permits and politics, not a lack of customers. Unlike April 2025, there is no single policy that can be reversed in a day: a national data center pause is unlikely to pass a split Congress, but states can act on their own.
cycle.for_you: Swing: stand aside until the index reclaims ground on rising volume. Puts: nothing passes today; cash is a position. Long term: the calm buy zone names (GD, LDOS, AEP, COF) held up; the falling chip names are watch names only.

principle.text: Don't let fear or the hope of a bargain make the decision; follow the rules you set when you were calm (paraphrase of Principles).
principle.applied: NVDA and AMD are 10% to 20% cheaper than a week ago, which feels like a bargain. The dashboard rule says the chart must be ready first, and today it is not.
